Two public trials, fitted both ways. The ASReml numbers on this page were
computed once with a licensed ASReml 4.2.0.392 under
R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31) on 2026-09-10, by
`data-raw/asreml_reference.R`, and stored with the package so this page
builds without a licence. Nothing here is quoted from memory or from a
manual.

The order is deliberate. First a case where the two agree, because a
comparison is worth nothing until you have seen that. Then the cases where
they do not, and why.

# 1. A whole alpha design: the two agree

`john.alpha` is the trial from the previous pages. Twenty-four genotypes,
three replicates, blocks nested in replicates.

| | ASReml | flexyBayes |
|---|---|---|
| call | `asreml(yield ~ rep, random = ~ rep:block + gen, data = john.alpha)` | `flexybayes(yield ~ rep, random = ~ rep:block + gen, data = john.alpha)` |
| heritability | `vpredict(m, h2 ~ V2/(V2 + V3))` | `vpredict(fit, h2 ~ sd_gen^2/(sd_gen^2 + sigma^2))` |

The `fixed` and `random` arguments are the same text. The heritability is
asked for the same way, and the name is the same, because it is ASReml's verb.


``` r
data(john.alpha, package = "agridat")

fit <- flexybayes(
  fixed   = yield ~ rep,
  random  = ~ rep:block + gen,
  data    = john.alpha,
  backend = "inla"
)
#> 
#> -- flexyBayes: INLA fit ----------------------------------------
#>   formula: yield ~ 1 + rep + f(rep_block_id, model = "iid", <prior: uniform-SD(0, 3.049)>) + f(gen, model = "iid", <prior: uniform-SD(0, 3.049)>)
#>   family:  gaussian
#> ------------------------------------------------------------

vpredict(fit, h2 ~ sd_gen^2 / (sd_gen^2 + sigma^2), n_draws = 4000)
#>   functional  estimate    median std.error conf.low conf.high
#> 1         h2 0.6376408 0.6407214 0.0998666 0.425785 0.8150101
```


``` r
rnd(asreml_ref$alpha[1, ])
#>                         design  n    h2    se lower upper
#> 1 24 genotypes, 3 reps (whole) 72 0.636 0.108 0.425 0.848
```

Heritability 0.64 either way, and the two intervals overlap almost exactly.
The variance components agree with `lme4::lmer()`'s REML fit of the same
model as well. On a trial of this size there is nothing to choose between
them, and any claim that there is should be treated with suspicion.

# 2. Shrink the trial, and one of them stops making sense

Now degrade the same trial: fewer genotypes, then plots dropped at random.
The whole-trial value of 0.64 is the target -- it is what the full design
says, and a method that recovers it from less data is doing well.

ASReml, from the stored run:


``` r
rnd(asreml_ref$alpha)
#>                           design  n    h2    se  lower upper
#> 1   24 genotypes, 3 reps (whole) 72 0.636 0.108  0.425 0.848
#> 2           12 genotypes, 3 reps 36 0.058 0.302 -0.533 0.649
#> 3            8 genotypes, 3 reps 24 0.177 0.385 -0.578 0.932
#> 4            6 genotypes, 3 reps 18 0.000 0.641 -1.256 1.256
#> 5 25% of plots dropped at random 54 0.491 0.179  0.141 0.841
#> 6 50% of plots dropped at random 36 0.408 0.305 -0.190 1.006
#> 7 65% of plots dropped at random 25 0.476 0.278 -0.069 1.020
```

Read the `lower` column. At twelve genotypes -- half the trial, and still a
real trial -- the interval runs from **-0.53**. At six it runs from -1.26 to
1.26, wider than the parameter space. Two of the random-deletion rows put the
upper bound above 1. A heritability is a proportion of variance and cannot be
negative or exceed one, so these intervals are not describing a heritability.
They are the delta method extrapolating a normal approximation off the end of
the parameter space, which is what it does when a variance component
approaches its boundary. ASReml is not doing anything wrong here. It is
reporting a standard error, and a standard error is a local quantity.

The same designs through flexyBayes:


``` r
degrade <- function(n_gen = NULL, drop_frac = NULL) {
  d <- john.alpha
  if (!is.null(n_gen)) {
    d <- droplevels(subset(d, gen %in% levels(d$gen)[seq_len(n_gen)]))
  }
  if (!is.null(drop_frac)) {
    set.seed(2026)
    d <- droplevels(d[-sample(nrow(d), round(drop_frac * nrow(d))), ])
  }
  d
}

designs <- list(
  "24 genotypes, 3 reps (whole)"    = degrade(),
  "12 genotypes, 3 reps"            = degrade(n_gen = 12),
  "6 genotypes, 3 reps"             = degrade(n_gen = 6),
  "50% of plots dropped at random"  = degrade(drop_frac = 0.50),
  "65% of plots dropped at random"  = degrade(drop_frac = 0.65)
)

out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(designs), function(nm) {
  f <- flexybayes(yield ~ rep, random = ~ rep:block + gen,
                  data = designs[[nm]], backend = "inla", verbose = FALSE)
  v <- vpredict(f, h2 ~ sd_gen^2 / (sd_gen^2 + sigma^2), n_draws = 4000)
  data.frame(design = nm, n = nrow(designs[[nm]]),
             h2 = v$estimate, lower = v$conf.low, upper = v$conf.high)
}))
rnd(out)
#>                           design  n    h2 lower upper
#> 1   24 genotypes, 3 reps (whole) 72 0.640 0.430 0.819
#> 2           12 genotypes, 3 reps 36 0.679 0.391 0.894
#> 3            6 genotypes, 3 reps 18 0.756 0.359 0.965
#> 4 50% of plots dropped at random 36 0.385 0.051 0.793
#> 5 65% of plots dropped at random 25 0.276 0.012 0.757
```

Every interval lies inside `[0, 1]`, because every draw does. They widen as
the design shrinks, which is the correct response to having less
information, and they keep containing the whole-trial value.

Two things must be said about this plainly.

The prior is doing work here, and it should be. With six genotypes the data
barely identifies a genetic variance, ASReml's REML estimate goes to the
boundary and reports zero, and the posterior sits well above it. If the truth
really were near zero the prior would be holding the estimate up wrongly. What
the posterior gives you is not a guarantee of being right -- it is an interval
you can act on, where the alternative is an interval that includes impossible
values.

And the point estimates are not the story. At 65 per cent deletion flexyBayes
returns a heritability some distance from the whole-trial figure. Its interval
still contains it, and still means what it says.

# 3. A multi-environment trial: the loadings get a posterior

`dasilva.maize` is nine environments, fifty-five genotypes, three replicates,
complete. The standard model is factor-analytic: one common factor across
environments, one variance specific to each, one residual variance per
environment.

| | ASReml | flexyBayes |
|---|---|---|
| random | `~ fa(env, 1):gen` | `~ fa(env, 1):gen` |
| residual | `~ dsum(~ units \| env)` | `~ dsum(~ units \| env)` |

Identical text. Both engines fit it, and they agree: the per-environment
residual standard deviations match to two decimals, and so do the specific
variances.

What differs is what comes back. ASReml returns a loading and a standard
error. flexyBayes returns a posterior for each loading, so any function of
them -- the quantity a breeder actually asks about -- has a posterior too.

The genetic correlation between two environments says whether they rank
genotypes the same way. Under a one-factor model it is a function of the
loadings and the specific variances, so it is one line:


``` r
data(dasilva.maize, package = "agridat")
d <- dasilva.maize[order(dasilva.maize$env, dasilva.maize$gen), ]

met <- flexybayes(yield ~ env, random = ~ fa(env, 1):gen,
                  residual = ~ dsum(~ units | env),
                  data = d, backend = "inla", verbose = FALSE)

vpredict(met,
  r_E5_E9 ~ (fa1_envE5 * sd_fa1) * (fa1_envE9 * sd_fa1) /
    sqrt(((fa1_envE5 * sd_fa1)^2 + sd_gen__envE5^2) *
         ((fa1_envE9 * sd_fa1)^2 + sd_gen__envE9^2)),
  r_E3_E8 ~ (fa1_envE3 * sd_fa1) * (fa1_envE8 * sd_fa1) /
    sqrt(((fa1_envE3 * sd_fa1)^2 + sd_gen__envE3^2) *
         ((fa1_envE8 * sd_fa1)^2 + sd_gen__envE8^2)),
  h2_E5 ~ ((fa1_envE5 * sd_fa1)^2 + sd_gen__envE5^2) /
          ((fa1_envE5 * sd_fa1)^2 + sd_gen__envE5^2 + sigma_E5^2),
  n_draws = 4000)
#>   functional  estimate    median std.error  conf.low conf.high
#> 1    r_E5_E9 0.6371187 0.6450666 0.1199627 0.3801449 0.8423240
#> 2    r_E3_E8 0.7981862 0.8211757 0.1206796 0.5054688 0.9619411
#> 3      h2_E5 0.5566210 0.5576646 0.0679189 0.4184597 0.6832296
```

The same three quantities from ASReml, by the delta method:


``` r
rnd(asreml_ref$met_derived)
#>   functional estimate    se lower upper
#> 1    r_E5_E9    0.777 0.131 0.519 1.034
#> 2    r_E3_E8    0.897 0.227 0.452 1.342
#> 3      h2_E5    0.570 0.072 0.429 0.712
```

The heritability, which is well identified, agrees: 0.57 against 0.55, with
near-identical intervals. The two correlations do not. Their delta-method
intervals reach **1.03** and **1.34**. A correlation cannot exceed one, and
these two are close enough to the boundary that a symmetric interval around
them leaves the parameter space. The posterior intervals stay inside it,
because a correlation computed on every draw is a correlation on every draw.

The same thing appears in the variance components themselves. Environment 8's
specific variance:


``` r
rnd(asreml_ref$met_varcomp[
  asreml_ref$met_varcomp$term == "fa(env, 1):gen!E8!var", ], 4)
#>                    term component     se     z
#> 8 fa(env, 1):gen!E8!var    0.0166 0.1369 0.121
```

An estimate of 0.017 with a standard error of 0.137. A variance, with a
standard error eight times its own size. flexyBayes reports that environment
as a standard deviation of 0.27 with an interval from 0.06 to 1.02 -- wide,
which is the honest answer, and positive throughout, which a variance must be.

# 4. What missing cells do, and do not, change

flexyBayes can keep a plot whose response was lost as a design row and treat
the response as a latent quantity (`na_action = "augment"`, the default),
rather than deleting the row. It is worth saying what that does.

On both trials on this page, and under deletion at random, it changes the
variance components hardly at all. That is not a disappointment, it is the
ignorability result: when the reason a value is missing is unrelated to the
value, the parameter posterior is the same whether the cell is carried or
dropped. The factor-analytic fit also does not fail on a design with whole
genotype-by-environment cells removed, which an earlier note in this project
predicted it would.

What carrying the cell does buy is the cell itself: a posterior for the
response that was not observed, on the same footing as the ones that were.
Where it would change the parameters is when the reason for the missingness
is related to the response -- the plot lost because it lodged, the trial
abandoned because it failed. That case is not demonstrated here, and it is
not claimed.

# What to take away

On a whole, well-sized trial the two approaches agree, and if you only ever
analyse whole trials the case for changing is weak.

The case is in three places. A quantity near a boundary -- a small variance
component, a high genetic correlation -- gets an interval that stays in the
parameter space instead of one that leaves it. A small or damaged trial gets
an interval that widens instead of a standard error whose
approximation has stopped holding. And any function of the variance
components is available exactly, from one line, instead of through a
linearisation.
